claims.text: The eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The lamellar microstructure is organized into colonies containing numerous internal boundaries.
The internal lamellar boundaries are prone to microcracking during room-temperature tensile deformation.
A minor boron addition during processing will segregate boron to the internal lamellar boundaries.
Boron segregation at lamellar boundaries enhances interfacial atomic bonding and cohesion.
Boron-enriched boundaries change failure from brittle interfacial decohesion to more uniform cohesive deformation.
Boron enrichment suppresses microcrack initiation at lamellar boundaries.
The boron-modified alloy will have higher room-temperature tensile strength than the unmodified baseline.
The boron-modified alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the unmodified baseline.
The unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy suffers a strength-ductility trade-off.
Brittle interfacial failure causes the baseline alloy's strength-ductility trade-off.
Excess boron can produce brittle boride phases that negate or worsen the mechanical properties.
Controlling cooling rate and annealing conditions can promote effective boron segregation at lamellar boundaries.
The optimum boron concentration and processing conditions remain to be established empirically.

contradictions.description: The claimed benefit is explicitly bounded to boron levels that do not form brittle borides, but boride formation is also treated as falsification. Boride-forming specimens would violate the stated boundary condition rather than directly test the hypothesis within its claimed domain.
